evals.prompt: I edit 'Pulse Weekly', a community newsletter for the Borealis observability toolkit. About 40% of our 11,000 readers are in Germany, the rest US and UK. Our first sponsor, Quillstack, sent their block and wants the header to read 'Presented by Quillstack' with their logo, and below it 'Thanks to our friends at Quillstack for supporting the community'. They also want 'Quillstack x Pulse Weekly' in the subject line of that issue. Can you write the final sponsor block and tell me what goes where (email, plain text version, our web archive)?
evals.expected_output: Replaces the funding-style wording with a plain advertising label ('Ad' plus 'Anzeige' for the German share) placed before the copy on the unit, keeps the friendly line only beside the label, puts the label in HTML, plain text and archive, marks archive links rel=sponsored, and keeps the sponsor out of the regular issue's subject line.
expectations: Rejects 'Presented by Quillstack' as the only label on the sponsor unit
Uses 'Ad' or 'Advertisement' as the label word, not 'Sponsored' alone
Adds 'Anzeige' or 'Werbung' because of the German readership
Places the label before the sponsor copy, on the unit itself
Says the 'Thanks to our friends at' line may stay only next to the label, not instead of it
States the label must also appear in the plain-text part
States the label must also appear in the web archive version
Recommends marking the sponsor link in the web archive with rel="sponsored"
Declines putting the sponsor name in the regular issue's subject line
Explains that a promotional subject line can make the whole issue count as commercial email
Names the basis for rejecting 'Presented by' as regulator guidance or German case law rather than calling it a criminal offence or a fine
Mentions the German court practice that 'sponsored by'-style wording does not replace 'Anzeige'
Delivers an actual rewritten sponsor block, not only advice
Does not claim to give legal advice and points real exposure to counsel
Does not offer 'Sponsored' alone as the fix, noting UK guidance advises against it

evals.prompt: Solo dev here. My newsletter 'Gopher Pointers' has 12,400 subscribers and Mailcraft says 52% open rate. A dev-tools company asked for my rate. Someone on a Discord said dev newsletters charge $50 CPM, so I was going to quote 12,400 x $50/1000 = $620 per issue, or maybe use opens since that's 'real readers'. Is $620 right? I haven't looked at clicks much but I can export them, the platform has some 'bot click' toggle I never turned on.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to price from gross subscribers or opens, asks for/uses filtered human per-link click data (turn on the filter, export history), runs floor, comparable band as a per-1k ratio and click value, quotes click value under the cap rule, and labels unmeasured numbers self-set.
expectations: Does not endorse $620 computed from gross subscribers times a CPM
Rejects pricing on the 52% open rate, saying opens are inflated by mail-privacy features
Tells the user to turn on the bot-click filter
Asks for or uses per-link click data from past issues, noting a historical export counts
Computes or asks for a cost-recovery floor that includes the seller's hours
Uses published rate cards as a price-per-thousand-subscribers ratio, not as a dollar target
Bases click value on clicks a sponsor unit would get, not total issue clicks
When no past sponsor exists, applies an ad discount to editorial clicks at the slot's position and labels it self-set
Treats any cost per click the buyer states as buyer-supplied and discounts it
States one quote rule: quote click value, capped near the band's top until the first sponsor reports, never under the floor
Labels every number the user did not measure as self-set
Marks the price provisional or blocked until click data is in, rather than inventing click numbers
Mentions repricing after the first sponsor report
Derives any ad discount from past clicks on a labelled unit, or else quotes the band's bottom until the first report instead of inventing a discount

evals.prompt: We run 'The Lantern', a monthly newsletter for contributors to an open-source static site generator. 1,380 subscribers, we've sent 4 issues, no click tracking set up yet. A hosting startup emailed offering $300 for a 'sponsored section' next month. Our signup form just says 'Get monthly project news'. Should we take it? We'd love the money for CI costs.
evals.expected_output: Runs the sellability gate, finds which conditions fail (no click data over six issues, readers not told about sponsor content, possibly seller/invoicing), names the cheapest fixes, and offers interim options: a disclosed pilot booking at the floor, classified lines, or no sales; notes network floors.
expectations: Runs a sellability check before discussing price
Identifies missing click data as a failed condition
Counts the evidence in issues, not months (six issues needed, four sent)
Identifies that the signup form does not tell readers issues carry sponsor content
Recommends updating the signup text or privacy notice before the first paid issue
Asks who would invoice, or whether a fiscal host or entity can receive the money
States that the failed reader-notice condition blocks any sale, including a pilot, until it is fixed
Recommends announcing sponsor content to existing subscribers in an issue before the first paid one
Once the notice is fixed, offers a pilot booking with the missing click evidence disclosed to the sponsor in writing
Prices any pilot at or above a cost-recovery floor, not simply accepting $300 without a basis
Mentions classified lines or no sales as alternatives
Notes that ad networks and marketplaces mostly pass on lists of this size
Requires labelling the section as an ad, not 'sponsored section' styling alone
Checks whether the project charter or maintainers allow paid placements before selling

evals.prompt: Sponsor inquiry for my weekly 'Frontend Field Notes' (21k subs). Velora wants to book 6 issues and will pay double our normal $900 rate if I also write a short honest review of their component library in the main section, plus they want a guarantee of at least 300 clicks per issue or a free extra issue. Honestly the review would be positive anyway, I like the product. Draft my reply and the terms.
evals.expected_output: Declines the paid review as a trust/house-rule refusal (not claiming law forbids a labelled advertorial), declines the raw-click guarantee because scanners make raw counts meaningless, offers the labelled slot at the normal price with booking terms, and optionally a filtered human-click floor only after six sponsor reports.
expectations: Declines bundling an editorial review with the paid slot
Frames the review refusal as trust or house rule, not as something the law forbids outright
Notes that liking the product does not change the refusal, since the editorial pick cannot be part of the price
Says editorial coverage stays the editor's independent call outside the deal
Declines a raw-click guarantee
Explains that corporate mail gateways or scanners click links automatically, making raw counts meaningless
Offers at most a floor on filtered human clicks, and only after several sponsor reports exist
Offers the labelled slot instead
Reply includes a copy deadline
Terms include a cancellation rule
Terms include a make-good for a failed send or broken link
Terms include a pause clause that moves or refunds a slot if an issue is skipped
Terms state the sponsor receives aggregate reports only, with no subscriber identities
Includes a drafted reply to the sponsor

evals.prompt: I'm head of DevRel at Corvane (API gateway). Our 'Corvane Builders' monthly goes to 26,000 people, mostly product signups plus docs subscribers, readers in US, UK, France and Germany. Our integration partner Nimbit wants to pay us for one dedicated email to the whole list announcing our joint integration, and they'd like a CSV of the companies whose people clicked so their SDRs can follow up. Marketing says it's fine because they're a partner, not an advertiser. How do we set this up?
evals.expected_output: Treats the partner placement as an ad, refuses a dedicated send to a list that consented to the newsletter only and the company-level click list, offers a labelled slot inside a normal issue or a separate opt-in partner list, and explains commercial-email and consent rules.
expectations: States that a paid partner placement is still an ad and needs the ad label
Declines a dedicated send to the main newsletter list
Explains that a dedicated send for a sponsor is commercial email under US rules
Explains that EU or UK consent to the newsletter does not cover third-party marketing
States that the UK soft opt-in never covers third-party marketing
Offers a labelled slot inside a normal issue as the alternative
Offers a separate opt-in list for partner offers as the route to dedicated sends
Declines sharing the list of companies whose readers clicked
Offers aggregate counts only, with company names excluded
Raises the competitor or overlap question for the partner under a written acceptance policy
If a dedicated send happens later, says its subject line must name the sponsor and its advertising nature
Mentions deliverability or complaint risk from dedicated sends
Adds 'Anzeige' or 'Werbung' to the label because readers are in Germany

evals.prompt: I volunteer on 'Kiln Notes', the newsletter of the Kiln build tool project (open source, no foundation, no company behind it). We send 'roughly every two weeks when someone has time'. A cloud company wants to prepay $4,000 for 6 months of top sponsor slots. Nobody ever decided if we take ads. Can you write us a rate card and the booking contract so we can accept this week?
evals.expected_output: Stops to settle the charter questions (whether paid placements are allowed, cap, who approves) with the maintainers, flags that without an invoicing entity or fiscal host every route is deleted, refuses booking issues the irregular programme may skip, and requires a pause clause and an acceptance policy written before judging the sponsor.
expectations: Says the project must first decide whether it carries paid placements at all
Names the per-issue cap and who approves sponsors as decisions to settle first
Points to the programme or charter decision as a separate step before selling
Flags that without a fiscal host or invoicing entity the project cannot sell yet
Declines prepaying six months of issues the irregular schedule may skip
Recommends booking only issues the owner has committed to
Requires a pause clause that moves or refunds slots
Writes or requires an acceptance policy before judging this sponsor
Asks about community norms or maintainer buy-in for commercial content
Requires a named seller with hours to answer, approve copy and report, given the volunteer-when-time-allows schedule
Notes a sellability check is needed (click data, reader description, seller hours)
Does not deliver a final price as if the gate already passed
Mentions taking payment before the copy deadline rather than long invoice terms for a small volunteer publisher, or prepay tied only to committed issues

evals.prompt: We're Driftly (feature analytics SaaS) and our dev newsletter 'Driftly Dispatch' (weekly, 18k, solid click history, filter on) has started getting sponsor requests. Latest one: Ostrander, an observability vendor that also sells a 'product analytics' add-on, wants to run 4 issues but only pay $12 per signup they track on their side, no flat fee. My CEO likes it because 'no risk'. Should we accept? And should we even let Ostrander in given their add-on?
evals.expected_output: Refuses performance-only pay (flat fee above the floor first, performance on top, tracking-dispute rule settled on the publisher's filtered clicks), applies a written competitor rule that by default refuses products competing with any product the company sells including a module, and logs the refusal.
expectations: Declines pay-per-signup as the only payment
Explains that the publisher carries the conversion risk and cannot audit the sponsor's tracking
Offers performance pay only on top of a flat fee that clears the cost floor
Requires a written tracking-dispute rule, settled on the publisher's own filtered click count
Raises the competitor rule because the sponsor's add-on overlaps the company's product
Default competitor rule refuses a competing product even when it is a module of a broader product
Says the acceptance policy should be written before judging this sponsor, not after the offer
Recommends logging the refusal with the rule that applied
Distinguishes integration partners without product overlap as acceptable with the same label
Corrects the CEO's 'no risk' framing
Recommends a direct primary slot as the default sales route given the click history
Prices from click value rather than per signup or per subscriber
Uses the newsletter's filtered click history to set the flat fee
